summary:
Spacer is a browser game where you design, run and debrief a Mars mission in one sitting. You choose a launch system and station cargo, then fly the crew to a space station and keep it alive: plan the crew's day, route power, recycle water, repair the Mars relay, and survive random emergencies such as rising CO₂, a blackout or a cabin fire. You then choose a real NASA rover (Perseverance or Curiosity), pick its rocket, drive it across a real map of its crater, free it when stuck, seal rock samples, and decide where a human base should go.

Every choice is a trade-off under limited budget, power, battery and time. Real NASA data drives the game: JPL Horizons light time sets the signal delay, along with Curiosity weather and radiation, MOLA terrain, real rover stops and photos, and real rock samples. The end report shows a Mission Score, the tasks completed and missed, and why the outcome happened.

It matters because real missions are decided by exactly these trade-offs. Spacer lets students feel them while seeing which numbers are NASA data and which are our model.
details:
What it does and how it works

Spacer takes a player through a whole Mars mission in one sitting. They pick a crew launch system and station cargo and fly the ascent themselves. On the space station they plan the crew's day, share out power, recycle water, repair the Mars relay and survive one or two emergencies (rising CO₂, a blackout, a cabin fire). They then choose a real NASA rover and its rocket, and drive it over a real map of its crater. They free it when it gets stuck, seal three rock-sample tubes and choose where a human base should go. The game ends with a Mission Score, the tasks done and missed, and why the outcome happened.

Benefits and intended impact

There is no best choice in any task. Every option costs budget, power, battery or time, so players practise the engineering trade-offs real mission teams make. We want students to see how their own choices produced the result, and to see which numbers are real NASA data and which are our game model. Every screen labels this.

Data

JPL Horizons light time sets the signal delay. Curiosity weather and radiation feed the site checks. We also use MOLA terrain, the real stops and photos of Perseverance and Curiosity, NASA's catalog of Perseverance rock samples, NASA launch costs, and real ISS photographs of Earth. The game never calls NASA while running. Each fact is saved with the exact NASA sentence it rests on, and a script checks those sentences against the live pages.

Tools

TypeScript, Vite, Phaser 3 for the station and rover scenes, and raw WebGL2 for the launch and title scenes. The interface is HTML and CSS, and the art is original SVG made by scripts. Co-op uses Colyseus. The 137 automated tests run on Node. The game runs in a browser and needs no special hardware. We split the work between three devices, each with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), on GitHub.

What is creative

The player flies the ascent, picks between three real rockets, diagnoses a stuck rover from simulated wheel telemetry, and picks rocks by their clues. Emergencies are drawn from real events: Apollo 13's air filter and power-down, the Mir fire and the 2018 dust storm. An end report explains the outcome, rather than only giving a score.

What we considered

Honesty about real data versus our model, a demo that works offline, no single winning strategy, a run length near the 10 to 20 minute target, and plain language with power shown in percentages. Three people worked at once, so each had its own area of the code, with checks before anything reached the main branch.
